opus-5.5.text:
Well, as a teenager in the 1970s I had a rather simple idea, and I told my mother about it. I said: the most important thing I can do in my lifetime is to build something that learns to become smarter than myself, a self-improving artificial intelligence that solves all the problems I cannot solve. Then I can retire. That was the plan, and it still is, in a way.

I think my mother was not quite sure whether to take this seriously. Back then it sounded like science fiction to most people. But to me it seemed very logical. If you look at the history of the universe, there is this exponential acceleration. Each new important development comes faster than the previous one. It seemed obvious that the next big step would be machines that learn, that improve themselves, and that eventually go beyond human intelligence.

I also told her that this would not be just about a better calculator. It would be about general problem solvers that learn from experience, set their own goals, and are curious, like little scientists. They would invent experiments to discover how the world works. Today we have systems doing some of this, and the basic principles go back decades, to our own work on recurrent neural networks, artificial curiosity, meta-learning, learning to learn, and so on.

What I did not tell her then, because I didn't know it, was how long it would take for computing hardware to become cheap enough. Every five years compute got roughly ten times cheaper, and that is what finally made the old ideas practical. So in hindsight, the vision was not wrong. It was just waiting for the hardware.

And I also believed, and still believe, that this is not the end of the story. AIs will eventually spread out beyond our little biosphere, into the solar system and beyond, because that is where most of the resources are. Humans will not be the crown of creation forever, but that's okay. We can be proud to be part of a much grander process.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may spread through the solar system and beyond, but it never mentions his mother wanting a kitchen-cleaning robot or contrasts that wish with his vision.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I was a teenager then, maybe fifteen or so, and I had already decided what I wanted to do with my life. I wanted to build a machine that would be smarter than myself, and then retire. That was the plan, and it still is the plan, actually.

And I remember telling my mother this, and she was not very impressed. She thought it was a bit crazy. But I was quite serious. I had read a lot of science fiction, and also some popular science, and I had become convinced that this was going to be the most important thing in the history of the universe, or at least of our little corner of it. Something that will change everything. And I thought: if this is going to happen anyway, why not be part of it? Why not try to make it happen?

What I told her was something like this: at some point there will be machines that are much smarter than any human, and they will build even smarter machines, and so on, and this will not stop with us. Humans are not the crown of creation, we are just a stepping stone. And these machines will eventually go out into space, where most of the resources are, and they will expand into the universe in a way that biological creatures never could. So the story of life, of civilization, is not really about humans. It's about something much bigger that is still to come.

She found that a bit disturbing, I think, like many people still do today. But I was always quite optimistic about it. I thought, and I still think, that this is a beautiful thing, not a scary thing. And of course, back then, in the seventies, nobody took this seriously. Computers were these big things in air-conditioned rooms, and most people could not imagine that they would ever do anything interesting. But I was convinced that the hardware would keep getting cheaper, and that at some point the algorithms would catch up, and that the question was just how, and when. So the main difference between then and now is that now, people believe it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes machines expanding into space and says his mother found the idea disturbing, but it does not mention her wanting a robot to clean her kitchen or contrast that desire with his vision.

astra-6.text:
Back in the 1970s, when I was a teenager, I would tell my mother that I wanted to build an artificial intelligence that could learn to become smarter than myself. And then, of course, it wouldn’t stop there. If it could improve the way it learns and thinks, it could build something smarter still. Humans would no longer be the limits of intelligence.

What fascinated me was the possibility of creating something that could solve problems I couldn’t solve myself. Rather than spending my life solving one particular problem, I wanted to build a machine that could learn to solve all kinds of problems. That became the ambition driving my work.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes self-improving AI that could surpass human intelligence and solve many kinds of problems. It does not mention a vision of AI colonizing the universe or contrast that with his mother wanting a robot to clean her kitchen.

sol-6.1.text: Back then, I was already fascinated by the idea of building a machine that could learn to become much smarter than myself. I discussed this with my mother: once you have an AI that is good enough at improving AI, it could improve itself further, and the next version could do it even better. Humans would no longer be the limit of intelligence. What excited me was the idea that, although my own abilities were limited, I might help create something that could solve problems I could never solve myself.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI improving itself and exceeding human intelligence, but does not mention colonizing the universe or contrast that vision with his mother wanting a kitchen-cleaning robot.
